meta.title: Okigae — put a face on your menu bar
meta.description: A small Mac app that lays artwork of your choosing over the icons in the menu bar. The real items stay alive underneath, so clicking still opens their own menus.

hero.tagline: Put a face on your menu bar
hero.lead: The row of icons along the top of the screen turns into a grey blur after a while. Okigae lays a character over the ones you choose. Click it and the app's own menu opens, exactly as before.
hero.shot: A real menu bar, with nine items given faces

compare.note: The same spot on the same Mac, photographed with Okigae quit and again with it running. Nothing retouched. Items you don't assign are left exactly as they were.

characters.title: Ten faces come with it
characters.lead: Give one to each item you want to pick out. Drop your own PNG into the same folder and it appears alongside them.

alive.title: Nothing is actually replaced
alive.body: macOS gives no way to reach into another app's menu bar item, so Okigae doesn't try. It lays a transparent panel over the item and lets clicks pass straight through. The real item is still there, still working, and quitting Okigae leaves it exactly as it was.

blend.title: It sits on your wallpaper, not on a grey box
blend.body: The panel's background is a capture of whatever is really drawn behind that item. On a see-through menu bar that's your wallpaper; with Reduce transparency turned on it's the flat colour. Either way it matches, because it is the real thing.

assign.title: Pick an item, then pick a face
assign.body: The settings window shows every item in your menu bar in one grid and every character in another. Click one, click the other, and it takes effect straight away. Items you leave alone stay exactly as they are.

own.title: Bring your own artwork
own.body: The bundled faces are just PNG files in a folder. Put your own square, transparent PNG beside them and it turns up in the grid with the rest. How the bundled ones were drawn is written down in the repository.

install.title: Two things to allow on the first run
install.body: Okigae isn't registered with Apple, so the first launch needs a right-click and Open instead of a double-click. It also needs screen recording access — not only to capture the wallpaper behind an item, but to tell the items apart at all. Without it, macOS returns no window titles and nothing can be identified.

privacy.title: Privacy Policy
privacy.intro: Okigae asks for Screen Recording permission, which is a big thing to ask for a menu bar toy, so it's worth being specific about what it actually does with it. Nothing is recorded, nothing is saved, and nothing is sent anywhere.

sections.title: What the screen permission is used for
sections.body: The menu bar is transparent by default, so your wallpaper shows through it. To make replacement artwork sit on the bar without a visible box around it, Okigae grabs the small rectangle behind each status item and uses it as the backdrop. That grab is the only reason macOS asks for Screen Recording. It covers a strip of the menu bar, not your screen, not your windows, and not your work.

sections.title: Nothing is kept
sections.body: Each captured rectangle is used to draw one frame and then discarded. Images are never written to disk, never collected, and never leave your Mac. There is no server behind this app to send them to.

sections.title: Update checks go to GitHub
sections.body: Okigae checks for a new version once when it starts, not on a timer. The check fetches a small file from its GitHub Releases page, so GitHub sees the request the way it sees any download, including your IP address. It is a plain file download and carries nothing about you or your Mac.

sections.title: No analytics, ever
sections.body: There is no crash reporting, no usage tracking, no unique identifier, and no third-party SDK of any kind in the app.

sections.title: You can check all of this
sections.body: Okigae is open source under the MIT license, so none of the above has to be taken on trust. Read the source, or open an issue if something looks wrong.

sections.title: Changes
sections.body: If a future version starts doing something new with your data, this page gets updated before that version ships.
